\chapter{It Has Happened}
\label{ch:ml-perfect}
\hlchaptermodality{111}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something has happened and still bears on now, not only that it happened.}

From cold: four shapes off one past form, and the word already in hand that finished the last of them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vanniṭṭŭ]{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്} — having come}

\label{lesson:ML-C111-vannittu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{he came}.

Then say the describing form you made from it — \emph{the teacher who came}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} (\emph{vanniṭṭŭ}) — \textbf{having come}.

It is the past form with \textbf{-\ml{ഇട്ട്}} put on the end.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വന്നു}} & he came \\
\textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} & having come \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one past form, two directions}]
\textbf{You have now made two things out of the same past form, and they were made in opposite ways.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വന്ന}} & the \textbf{\ml{ു}} taken \textbf{off} — describes a noun \\
\textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} & \textbf{-\ml{ഇട്ട്}} put \textbf{on} — leans toward a verb \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The describing form was made by taking a vowel sign away. This one is made by adding, and what it reaches for is different: \textbf{\ml{വന്ന}} wants a noun to sit in front of, while \textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} wants something else to follow — another verb, or the word that closes the sentence.

\textbf{On its own it feels unfinished, and that is the point.} Saying \emph{vanniṭṭŭ} and stopping leaves a listener waiting, the way \emph{having come} does in English. The next page gives it the word it is waiting for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{വന്നു}}, then \textbf{\ml{വന്ന}}, then \textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}}
  \item which of the three was made by taking something away
  \item which of the three leaves a listener waiting
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is added to a past form to make this one? (\textbf{-\ml{ഇട്ട്}}.) What does \textbf{\ml{വന്ന}} want in front of it? (\textbf{A noun.}) What does \textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} want after it? (\textbf{Another word to finish the sentence.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vanniṭṭuṇṭŭ]{\ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്} — he has come}

\label{lesson:ML-C111-vannittundu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{having come}.

Then say the word that means \emph{there is} — the one that also does \emph{somebody has}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{അവൻ} \ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{avan vanniṭṭuṇṭŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{He has come.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Put the two together and nothing is left over.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} & having come \\
\textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}} & there is \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

They run together in speech into \textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}}, and that is the whole of the construction: the waiting form, and the word it was waiting for.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word you already knew did the work}]
\textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}} was given to you as \emph{there is} and \emph{somebody has}. That second job is the one showing here. English builds its perfect on \textbf{have} — \emph{he has come} — and Malayalam reaches for the word it already uses for having.

So the two languages land in the same place from the same starting point, which is worth noticing precisely because so little else about the two verbs lines up.

\textbf{What it says that a plain past does not} is that the coming is done and bears on now. \emph{avan vannu} reports the event. \emph{avan vanniṭṭuṇṭŭ} tells you he is here — the arriving happened, and you are being told about its result.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{അവൻ} \ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}}
  \item the two pieces it is made of, separately
  \item which English word Malayalam is matching when it reaches for \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{He has come}? (\textbf{\ml{അവൻ} \ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}}.) What two pieces is it built from? (\textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} and \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}}.) Which of \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}}'s two jobs is doing the work? (\textbf{Having.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\ml{വന്നു} — \ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}}

\label{lesson:ML-C111-past-or-perfect}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{he came}, then \emph{he has come}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which one a situation asks for}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അവൻ} \ml{വന്നു}} & reports the event \\
\textbf{\ml{അവൻ} \ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}} & reports where that leaves things \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Both are true of the same arrival.} Which you pick depends on what the person listening needs: whether you are telling them what happened, or telling them how matters stand because of it.

A useful test while the difference is settling: if you could follow your sentence with \emph{…so he is here now} without repeating yourself, the second form was the one you wanted.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item somebody asks whether the teacher is here — answer with \textbf{\ml{അവൻ} \ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}}
  \item somebody asks what happened yesterday — answer with \textbf{\ml{അവൻ} \ml{വന്നു}}
  \item both sentences one after the other, and name the piece that differs
  \item the middle piece on its own — \textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} — and stop, hearing how it waits
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form reports the event itself? (\textbf{\ml{വന്നു}}.) Which reports how things stand now? (\textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}}.) How many new words did choosing between them need? (\textbf{None.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[naalu roopam]{(vannu, vanna, vanniṭṭŭ, vanniṭṭuṇṭŭ) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R111-perfect-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{having come}, then \emph{he has come}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four shapes off one past form}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വന്നു}} & he came \\
\textbf{\ml{വന്ന}} & that came — a vowel sign taken \textbf{off} \\
\textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ട്}} & having come — \textbf{-\ml{ഇട്ട്}} put \textbf{on} \\
\textbf{\ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}} & he has come — that, plus \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Every row after the first is the row above it with one change.} Nothing in this chapter asked you to learn a word; it asked you to notice what a form you already had could be turned into.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You could say that something happened, and not that it has happened.} The difference matters more than it looks: answering \emph{is he here?} with the plain past reports yesterday, and leaves the question standing.

The word that closed the gap was one you had held for a long time. \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}} was given to you as \emph{there is} and \emph{somebody has}, and it is the second job that builds this. English does the same thing with \emph{have}, which is a coincidence worth having noticed, because very little else about the two verbs matches.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all four shapes, in the order of the table
  \item which one was made by taking something away
  \item which word finishes the last one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{He has come}? (\textbf{\ml{അവൻ} \ml{വന്നിട്ടുണ്ട്}}.) What is added to a past form to start it? (\textbf{-\ml{ഇട്ട്}}.) What finishes it? (\textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}}.) How many new words did this chapter cost? (\textbf{None.})
\end{tcolorbox}
